title: Directional Gradient Projection for Robust Fine-Tuning of Foundation Models

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to improve robust fine-tuning of foundation models by addressing underfitting and heavy hyper-parameter tuning in prior magnitude-based weight-projection methods that ignore gradient direction. Paper [3] explicitly discusses robust fine-tuning and highlights limitations of projected gradient descent methods, including scalability issues and constraints that hinder broader adoption. Paper [15] also addresses robust fine-tuning challenges, particularly the degradation of performance under distribution shifts, and critiques hand-crafted regularization techniques. Both papers share the same high-level objective of improving robust fine-tuning, making the purpose covered.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, Directional Gradient Projection (DiGraP), reframes robust fine-tuning as multi-objective optimization, dynamically learning the priority between task loss and L2-SP regularization by projecting conflicting gradients orthogonally with a trainable strength parameter. Paper [7] introduces a multi-objective optimization approach for conflicting objectives, reformulating gradient updates to minimize interference, which aligns with the primitive of resolving gradient conflicts through projection. Paper [8] also addresses conflicting gradients in multi-task learning, proposing conflict-averse gradient descent, which similarly resolves gradient interference. Paper [5] adapts PCGrad for multitask learning, incorporating gradient projection and task prioritization, which matches the primitive of gradient projection with dynamic weighting. These papers collectively cover the mechanism.

### Evaluation
The evaluation demonstrates DiGraP's consistent outperformance of baselines across image classification and VQA tasks, improving both ID generalization and OOD robustness. Papers [28] and [29] introduce OOD-CV benchmarks for evaluating robustness to out-of-distribution shifts in natural images, which align with the evaluation design of benchmarking OOD robustness in vision tasks. Paper [24] introduces Adversarial VQA, a benchmark for evaluating robustness in VQA models, which matches the evaluation design for vision-language tasks. These prior papers use similar benchmark families and metric semantics, covering the evaluation design.

### Domain
The domain is robust fine-tuning of foundation models in vision and vision-language applications. Papers [3], [4], [10], and [15] all address robust fine-tuning of foundation models, specifically targeting vision or vision-language tasks. Paper [10] focuses on robust fine-tuning for pre-trained 3D point cloud models, which is a subdomain of vision. Paper [4] addresses robust fine-tuning for vision-language models, improving OOD generalization and confidence calibration. These papers collectively cover the domain.

**PURPOSE: Improve robust fine-tuning of foundation models, avoiding underfitting and heavy hyper-parameter tuning of prior magnitude-based weight-projection methods that ignore gradient direction.**

Paper [1] "Trainable Projected Gradient Method for Robust Fine-Tuning" explicitly addresses the problem of "manually crafted heuristics or expensive hyper-parameter searches" in robust fine-tuning, proposing a trainable method. Paper [3] "Fast Trainable Projection for Robust Fine-Tuning" also targets "two limitations prevent this method from being adopted more widely, scalab[ility]" in projected gradient descent for robust fine-tuning. Both share the same objective: improve robust fine-tuning by replacing manual/expensive hyper-parameter tuning in projection-based methods. The contribution's purpose is substantively equivalent to [1] and [3].

---

**MECHANISM: Directional Gradient Projection (DiGraP) — reframes robust fine-tuning as multi-objective optimization (task loss + L2-SP), projects conflicting gradients onto orthogonal directions, with a trainable scalar omega ∈ [0,1] controlling projection strength per layer.**

Paper [16] "Gradient Surgery for Multi-Task Learning" introduces PCGrad, which projects one task's gradient onto the orthogonal complement of another's when they conflict (negative cosine similarity) — the same core primitive of orthogonal gradient projection under conflict. Paper [5] "Task Weighting through Gradient Projection for Multitask Learning" extends PCGrad with task prioritization/weighting, adapting projection strength — analogous to the trainable omega. Paper [8] "Conflict-Averse Gradient Descent for Multi-task Learning" also addresses conflicting gradients in multi-task settings with projection. Paper [1] introduces a trainable projected gradient method for robust fine-tuning. The combination of (a) orthogonal projection under gradient conflict [16] and (b) trainable projection strength [5] and (c) applied to robust fine-tuning [1] covers the mechanism's primitives. Paper [16] is the clearest match for the core orthogonal-projection-under-conflict primitive; [5] covers the trainable weighting of projection strength.

---

**EVALUATION: Outperforms baselines on image classification and VQA tasks with discriminative and generative backbones, measuring ID and OOD accuracy.**

Paper [1] evaluates robust fine-tuning methods on image classification benchmarks measuring ID and OOD accuracy, comparing against baselines. Paper [3] similarly evaluates on image classification with ID/OOD metrics. Paper [4] "Towards Calibrated Robust Fine-Tuning of Vision-Language Models" evaluates on vision-language models with OOD generalization metrics. The evaluation design — comparing robust fine-tuning methods on standard image classification benchmarks with ID/OOD accuracy metrics — is well-established in [1], [3], and [4]. VQA evaluation for robustness appears in [24]. The design (benchmark family: ImageNet variants + OOD shifts; metric: ID/OOD accuracy; comparison against baselines) is covered by [1] and [3].

---

**DOMAIN: Robust fine-tuning of foundation models (vision / vision-language).**

Paper [1] operates in robust fine-tuning of vision foundation models. Paper [3] is identical in domain. Paper [4] covers vision-language models specifically. This domain is thoroughly covered.

### Purpose
The contribution aims to extend robust fine-tuning evaluation from uni-modal settings to multi-modal (VQA) settings with a principled OOD categorization. Paper [1] explicitly addresses OOD detection in multimodal VQA tasks, benchmarking methods for handling OOD samples in vision-and-language settings. Paper [2] discusses robust fine-tuning for vision-language models, improving OOD generalization and confidence calibration. Paper [3] introduces VQA-GEN, a multi-modal benchmark for distribution shifts in VQA, focusing on both visual and textual domains. Paper [11] discusses robust VQA methods and datasets, emphasizing OOD generalization challenges. These papers share the same high-level objective of improving or evaluating OOD robustness in multimodal VQA tasks, making the purpose covered.

### Mechanism
The contribution constructs new evaluation settings, including an Image-Classification-reformulated VQA benchmark bridging uni-modal and multi-modal, and categorizes ten OOD VQA datasets into ID, near-OOD, and far-OOD by distribution-shift type and degree. Paper [3] introduces VQA-GEN, a multi-modal benchmark for distribution shifts, which includes textual and visual shifts, aligning with the idea of categorizing datasets by distribution shift type. Paper [15] introduces Adversarial VQA, a benchmark collected iteratively via adversarial procedures, which also categorizes datasets based on robustness challenges. Paper [5] proposes a semi-automatic framework for generating disentangled shifts in VQA datasets, addressing multi-modal distribution shifts. These mechanisms align with the contribution's approach to categorizing datasets and constructing benchmarks, making the mechanism covered.

### Evaluation
The contribution provides a consistent comparative analysis of robust fine-tuning algorithms across the ten categorized VQA datasets. Paper [1] benchmarks OOD detection methods in multimodal VQA tasks, using a suite of datasets for comparative analysis. Paper [3] evaluates VQA-GEN across multiple models and datasets, providing a comparative analysis of domain generalization performance. Paper [11] discusses robust VQA methods and datasets, emphasizing evaluation across diverse datasets for OOD generalization. Paper [15] evaluates VQA robustness using the Adversarial VQA benchmark, providing comparative analysis across models. These papers use similar evaluation designs (benchmarking across datasets for comparative analysis), making the evaluation covered.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of robust fine-tuning evaluation for VQA/vision-language tasks. Paper [1] focuses on OOD detection in multimodal VQA tasks. Paper [2] addresses robust fine-tuning for vision-language models. Paper [3] introduces a multi-modal benchmark for VQA domain generalization. Paper [11] discusses robust VQA methods and datasets. Paper [15] introduces a benchmark for evaluating VQA robustness. All these papers operate in the same general application area of robust evaluation for VQA/vision-language tasks, making the domain covered.
